notes:
Classification & Nomenclature

  • Compounds classified as acyclic (open chain), alicyclic (carbocyclic, non-aromatic ring) and aromatic. Functional groups fix IUPAC suffix priority: acids > anhydrides > esters > amides > nitriles > aldehydes > ketones > alcohols > amines > ethers.
  • Lowest locants are given to the principal characteristic group first, then to substituents/unsaturation as a set.

Electronic Displacement Effects

EffectNatureExample
Inductive (I)Permanent, through $\sigma$ bonds, distance-dependent-NO$_2$, -COOH: $-I$; alkyl: $+I$
Resonance (R)Delocalisation of $\pi$/lone pair, permanent-OH, -NH$_2$ on benzene: $+R$
Electromeric (E)Temporary, needs attacking reagent, complete transfer of $\pi$ electron pairAddition to C=C
Hyperconjugation$\sigma(\text{C-H})$ to empty/partial p-orbital overlapStabilises carbocations, alkenes
  • Stability order of carbocations/free radicals: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl (more hyperconjugation/+I from alkyl groups).
  • Acidity: more $-I$/$-R$ withdrawing groups on the acid or its conjugate base increase acidity (e.g. Cl-CH$_2$-COOH > CH$_3$COOH). Basicity of amines depends on availability of the lone pair (aliphatic > NH$_3$ > aromatic amines, since the lone pair on aniline delocalises into the ring).

Reaction Types & Intermediates

  • Substitution (replace an atom/group), Addition (across multiple bond), Elimination (form multiple bond, lose small molecule), Rearrangement (skeleton reorganises, e.g. via carbocation).
  • Reagents: Electrophiles (electron-loving, e.g. NO$_2^+$, Br$^+$, carbocations) and Nucleophiles (electron-rich, e.g. OH$^-$, CN$^-$, NH$_3$).
  • Carbocation: sp$^2$, planar, electron deficient. Carbanion: sp$^3$, pyramidal, lone pair. Free radical: odd electron, formed by homolysis.

Purification

  • Simple distillation (liquids, large b.p. difference); fractional distillation (close b.p. liquids); steam distillation (steam-volatile, water-immiscible liquids); distillation under reduced pressure (high b.p., decomposable liquids).
  • Crystallisation: purify solids using difference in solubility. Sublimation: solid directly to vapour (e.g. camphor, naphthalene).
  • Chromatography: separation by differential adsorption/partition between stationary and mobile phase (column, TLC, paper).

Qualitative & Quantitative Analysis

  • Lassaigne's test fuses the compound with Na to convert N, S, halogens to NaCN, Na$_2$S, NaX (covalent → ionic) for detection (Prussian blue for N, purple/violet with sodium nitroprusside for S, AgX precipitate for halogens).
  • Duma's method: N estimated as N$_2$ gas by CuO oxidation. Kjeldahl's method: N converted to (NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$, distilled with NaOH into standard acid, back-titrated (not for N in nitro/azo/ring N compounds).
  • Carius method: halogens/S estimated by fuming HNO$_3$ + AgNO$_3$ (as AgX) or BaCl$_2$ (as BaSO$_4$).
  • %C, H by combustion: mass of CO$_2$ and H$_2$O formed gives %C and %H.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 2-3 questions from this chapter, mostly on electronic effects (stability/acidity ordering), reaction intermediates, and one on analysis methods (Lassaigne's/Kjeldahl/Carius). Learn the effect-vs-example table cold.

questions.q: The correct decreasing order of stability of the following carbocations: (I) $CH_3^+$ (II) $(CH_3)_3C^+$ (III) $(CH_3)_2CH^+$ is
questions.explanation: More alkyl groups give more hyperconjugation and +I effect, so 3° > 2° > 1° i.e. II > III > I.
questions.trick: Stability order: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl carbocation, always.

questions.q: Which of the following shows the electromeric effect?
options: Permanent polarisation of a C-Cl bond
Complete transfer of a $\pi$ electron pair to one atom on attack by a reagent
Polarity due to unequal sharing of $\sigma$ electrons
Delocalisation of the lone pair on -OH attached to benzene
questions.explanation: The electromeric effect is a temporary effect operating only in the presence of an attacking reagent, involving complete transfer of a shared $\pi$ electron pair to one of the atoms.
questions.trick: Electromeric = complete $\pi$-shift, only happens WHEN reagent attacks.

questions.q: Which compound is expected to be the strongest acid?
questions.explanation: Each additional electronegative Cl increases the $-I$ effect, withdrawing electron density and stabilising the conjugate base more, so trichloroacetic acid is the strongest.
questions.trick: More Cl/EWG on acid → stronger $-I$ → stronger acid.

questions.q: The correct order of basicity in the gas/solution phase comparison (aliphatic amine vs ammonia vs aniline) is
questions.explanation: In methylamine the +I effect of -CH$_3$ increases electron density on N; in aniline the lone pair delocalises into the ring (resonance), reducing its availability. So methylamine > ammonia > aniline.
questions.trick: +I raises basicity, resonance (aniline) lowers it: alkyl-NH$_2$ > NH$_3$ > aniline.

questions.q: A carbanion is best described as
options: sp$^3$ hybridised, with a positive charge on carbon
sp$^3$ hybridised, pyramidal, with a lone pair
sp hybridised, linear, with an odd electron
questions.explanation: A carbanion carbon is sp$^3$ hybridised, pyramidal (like NH$_3$), and carries a lone pair of electrons giving it a negative charge.
questions.trick: Carbanion = like NH$_3$: sp$^3$, pyramidal, lone pair.

questions.q: IUPAC name of CH$_3$-CH(OH)-CH$_2$-CHO is
questions.explanation: Numbering from the -CHO carbon (C1) gives -OH at C3: the principal chain is butanal with a 3-hydroxy substituent, i.e. 3-hydroxybutanal.
questions.trick: Number from the -CHO end so it gets C1; count OH position from there.

questions.q: In Lassaigne's test, nitrogen present in an organic compound is converted into
questions.explanation: Fusion of the organic compound with sodium metal converts covalently bound N (with C) into sodium cyanide, NaCN, which is then detected as Prussian blue.
questions.trick: Lassaigne fusion: N (with C, Na) always gives NaCN.

questions.q: Kjeldahl's method cannot be used to estimate nitrogen in
questions.explanation: In Kjeldahl's method the nitrogen must be converted to ammonium sulphate on heating with H$_2$SO$_4$; nitrogen present as nitro, azo or in a ring (pyridine-type) is not quantitatively converted, so the method fails for such compounds.
questions.trick: Kjeldahl fails when N can't become NH$_4^+$: nitro, azo, ring N.

questions.q: 0.24 g of an organic compound on Carius estimation gave 0.4785 g of AgBr. The percentage of bromine in the compound is (Ag = 108, Br = 80, AgBr = 188)
questions.trick: %Br $=\dfrac{\text{wt AgBr}\times80}{188\times\text{wt sample}}\times100$.

questions.q: Which technique is used to separate a mixture of two miscible liquids whose boiling points differ by less than 25 K?
questions.explanation: When boiling points are close, repeated vaporisation-condensation on a fractionating column (fractional distillation) is needed for good separation; simple distillation only works when the difference is large.
questions.trick: Close boiling points (<25 K apart) → fractional distillation, not simple.

questions.q: Steam distillation is applicable to a liquid that is
options: soluble in water at all proportions
miscible with water and decomposes near its boiling point
immiscible with water, steam-volatile and has appreciable vapour pressure at 373 K
questions.explanation: Steam distillation works for substances that are insoluble in water, steam-volatile, and possess some vapour pressure at 373 K, allowing them to distil below their normal boiling point along with steam.
questions.trick: Steam distillation needs: water-insoluble + volatile + some vapour pressure at 373 K.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a nucleophile?
questions.explanation: CN$^-$ has a lone pair and negative charge, so it is electron-rich and attacks electron-deficient centres — a nucleophile. NO$_2^+$, BF$_3$ and H$^+$ are all electrophiles.
questions.trick: Nucleophile = negative/lone-pair species; spot the one with extra electrons.

questions.q: Which functional group has the highest priority for suffix naming (senior-most) among the following?
questions.explanation: In IUPAC seniority for suffixes, carboxylic acids rank above aldehydes, alcohols and amines, so -COOH is named as the principal characteristic group.
questions.trick: Suffix seniority: COOH > CHO > OH > amine — acid always wins.

questions.q: Column chromatography separates components of a mixture mainly on the basis of
options: their differential adsorption on a stationary phase as a mobile phase moves through it
questions.explanation: In chromatography, components distribute differently between a stationary phase and a moving mobile phase (adsorption/partition), and travel at different rates, effecting separation.
questions.trick: Chromatography = differential adsorption/partition between stationary and mobile phase.

questions.q: The percentage of hyperconjugation-stabilised species increases with the number of $\alpha$-hydrogens. Among $CH_3-CH_2^+$ (I) and $(CH_3)_2CH^+$ (II), the number of hyperconjugating C-H bonds are respectively
questions.explanation: In CH$_3$-CH$_2^+$ the single adjacent CH$_3$ group has 3 $\alpha$ C-H bonds, giving 3 hyperconjugating structures. In (CH$_3)_2$CH$^+$ the cationic carbon has two adjacent CH$_3$ groups, each with 3 $\alpha$ C-H bonds, giving $3\times2=6$ hyperconjugating C-H bonds.
questions.trick: Count $\alpha$ C-H bonds: each adjacent CH$_3$ contributes 3 hyperconjugating structures.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs represents a substitution and an elimination reaction respectively?
questions.explanation: CH$_3$Br + OH$^-$ replaces Br by OH (substitution); C$_2$H$_5$Br with alcoholic KOH removes HBr to form a double bond (elimination).
questions.trick: OH$^-$/water attacking = substitution; alcoholic KOH = elimination (removes HX).

questions.q: Which technique would best separate naphthalene (which sublimes) from an involatile solid impurity?
questions.explanation: Naphthalene sublimes on heating, passing directly to vapour and leaving the non-volatile impurity behind; cooling the vapour gives pure naphthalene.
questions.trick: Solid that vaporises directly without melting → separate by sublimation.

questions.q: In the free radical Cl$_2$/CH$_4$ reaction, the propagation step Cl• + CH$_4$ → •CH$_3$ + HCl illustrates
options: a step where a bond is broken homolytically to generate a new radical
questions.explanation: Free-radical propagation proceeds by homolytic C-H bond cleavage: Cl• abstracts an H atom, generating HCl and a new methyl free radical, each fragment keeping one electron.
questions.trick: Radical propagation = homolytic bond cleavage generating a new radical.

questions.q: Which of the following alkyl groups shows the strongest $+I$ effect at its point of attachment: -C(CH$_3$)$_3$, -CH(CH$_3$)$_2$, -CH$_2$CH$_3$, -CH$_3$?
questions.explanation: The +I (electron-releasing) effect of alkyl groups increases with branching/chain length: tertiary butyl group -C(CH$_3$)$_3$ has the strongest +I effect among these.
questions.trick: +I effect grows with branching: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.

questions.q: 0.30 g of an organic compound gave 0.66 g of CO$_2$ and 0.27 g of H$_2$O on combustion. The percentage of carbon in the compound is (C = 12, molar mass CO$_2$ = 44)
questions.trick: %C $=\dfrac{\text{wt CO}_2\times12}{44\times\text{wt sample}}\times100$.

questions.q: The number of chain (skeletal) isomers possible for pentane, C$_5$H$_{12}$, is
questions.explanation: C$_5$H$_{12}$ has 3 chain isomers: n-pentane, 2-methylbutane (isopentane) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane).
questions.trick: CₙH$_{2n+2}$ chain isomers: pentane has exactly 3 (n-, iso-, neo-).

questions.q: Ethanol (CH$_3$CH$_2$OH) and dimethyl ether (CH$_3$OCH$_3$) both have molecular formula C$_2$H$_6$O. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Same molecular formula but different functional groups (-OH in an alcohol vs -O- in an ether) is functional isomerism.
questions.trick: Same formula, different functional group (OH vs O) = functional isomerism.

questions.q: Diethyl ether (C$_2$H$_5$-O-C$_2$H$_5$) and methyl propyl ether (CH$_3$-O-C$_3$H$_7$) are related by
questions.explanation: Both belong to the same class (ethers, same functional group) but differ in the alkyl groups attached to the functional atom — this is metamerism.
questions.trick: Same functional group, different alkyl groups either side = metamerism.

questions.q: Acetone (CH$_3$COCH$_3$) exists in equilibrium with a small amount of its enol form, CH$_3$-C(OH)=CH$_2$. This keto-enol equilibrium is an example of
questions.explanation: Tautomers are constitutional isomers that interconvert rapidly and exist in equilibrium, typically differing in the position of a proton and a double bond (here keto $\rightleftharpoons$ enol).
questions.trick: Rapid keto $\rightleftharpoons$ enol interconversion is the classic tautomerism example.

questions.q: The degree of unsaturation of a hydrocarbon with molecular formula C$_4$H$_6$ is
questions.explanation: Degree of unsaturation $= \dfrac{2C+2-H}{2} = \dfrac{2(4)+2-6}{2} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2$, consistent with a diene or an alkyne such as but-1-yne.
questions.trick: DoU $=\dfrac{2C+2-H}{2}$ (add N, ignore halogens like H).

questions.q: The correct order of C-C-C bond angles in sp$^3$, sp$^2$ and sp hybridised carbon centres is
questions.explanation: Bond angles are 109.5° (sp$^3$), 120° (sp$^2$) and 180° (sp), so the order is sp > sp$^2$ > sp$^3$.
questions.trick: More s-character → wider angle: sp(180°) > sp$^2$(120°) > sp$^3$(109.5°).

questions.q: While drawing resonance structures for a species, which structure contributes MOST to the resonance hybrid (is most stable)?
options: Any structure that requires bond breaking without electron reorganisation
The one with the maximum number of formal charges of the same sign adjacent to each other
The one with the greatest number of covalent bonds and least separation of charge
The one with a negative charge on the least electronegative atom
questions.explanation: A resonance structure is more stable (contributes more) when it has more covalent bonds, less charge separation, and negative charge on a more electronegative atom, with like charges kept apart.
questions.trick: Best resonance structure: max covalent bonds, min charge separation.

questions.q: In Duma's method, 0.14 g of an organic compound gave 22.4 mL of N$_2$ gas measured at STP. The percentage of nitrogen in the compound is
questions.explanation: Moles of N$_2$ $= 22.4/22400 = 0.001$ mol, giving mass of N $= 0.001\times28 = 0.028$ g (28 g of N per mole of N$_2$). %N $= \dfrac{0.028}{0.14}\times100 = 20\%$.
questions.trick: Duma's: 22400 mL N$_2$ at STP = 28 g N; scale down from there.

questions.q: In the Carius method, 0.20 g of an organic compound containing sulphur gave 0.466 g of BaSO$_4$. The percentage of sulphur in the compound is (S = 32, BaSO$_4$ = 233)
questions.trick: %S $=\dfrac{\text{wt BaSO}_4\times32}{233\times\text{wt sample}}\times100$.

questions.q: In paper chromatography, a spot moves 3 cm while the solvent front moves 10 cm from the point of application. The R$_f$ value of the spot is
questions.explanation: $R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by solute}}{\text{distance moved by solvent}} = \dfrac{3}{10} = 0.3$.
questions.trick: $R_f=\dfrac{\text{distance by solute}}{\text{distance by solvent front}}$, always <1.

questions.q: Glycerol is purified by distillation under reduced pressure mainly because
options: it decomposes near/before reaching its normal boiling point at atmospheric pressure
questions.explanation: Lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point, so a high-boiling liquid like glycerol, which would decompose at its normal (atmospheric) boiling point, can be distilled safely at a lower temperature.
questions.trick: Lower pressure lowers b.p. — use it to distil heat-sensitive high-boilers.

questions.q: Differential extraction is used to separate a compound from its aqueous solution by shaking it with an organic solvent because the compound is
options: more soluble in the organic solvent than in water, and can be repeatedly extracted with fresh portions
insoluble in both the aqueous and organic layers
questions.explanation: Differential (solvent) extraction relies on the compound being more soluble in an immiscible organic solvent than in water; repeated extraction with fresh solvent recovers it more completely than a single extraction.
questions.trick: Multiple small extractions beat one big one — think partition coefficient.

questions.q: The reaction Cl$_2$ $\to$ 2Cl• (under UV light) is an example of
questions.explanation: Since Cl$_2$ is a symmetrical, non-polar bond, it breaks homolytically under UV light, with each Cl atom retaining one electron to form two free radicals.
questions.trick: Symmetrical non-polar bond + UV → homolysis into two radicals.

questions.q: Although each C-Cl bond is polar, CCl$_4$ has zero net dipole moment because
options: the four C-Cl bond dipoles are symmetrically (tetrahedrally) arranged and cancel each other
questions.explanation: In the tetrahedral CCl$_4$ molecule the four identical, symmetrically directed C-Cl bond dipoles cancel vectorially, giving a net dipole moment of zero, unlike CHCl$_3$ where the asymmetry leaves a resultant dipole.
questions.trick: Symmetric tetrahedral bond dipoles cancel → CCl$_4$ has zero net dipole.

questions.q: Among 2-chlorobutanoic acid, 3-chlorobutanoic acid and 4-chlorobutanoic acid, the correct order of acid strength is
questions.explanation: The $-I$ effect of chlorine falls off rapidly with distance from the -COOH group, so the closer the Cl substituent is to the carboxyl carbon, the more it withdraws electron density and stabilises the conjugate base: 2-chloro > 3-chloro > 4-chloro.
questions.trick: $-I$ effect dies off with distance: closer halogen to COOH = stronger acid.

questions.q: Which of the following free radicals is expected to be the MOST stable?
questions.explanation: The allyl radical is stabilised by resonance (delocalisation of the odd electron over two carbons through the adjacent $\pi$ bond), making it more stable than simple alkyl radicals which are stabilised only by hyperconjugation.
questions.trick: Resonance-stabilised (allylic/benzylic) radical beats hyperconjugation-only radicals.

questions.q: The cyclopropenyl cation (a 3-membered ring with 2 $\pi$ electrons) is aromatic according to Hückel's rule because it is
options: planar, cyclic, fully conjugated with $(4n+2)\pi$ electrons for n = 0 (2 $\pi$ electrons)
questions.explanation: It is planar, cyclic and fully conjugated with 2 $\pi$ electrons, satisfying $(4n+2)$ with n = 0, so despite being a non-benzenoid, 3-membered system it is aromatic.
questions.trick: Check planar + cyclic + conjugated + $(4n+2)\pi$ e⁻ for aromaticity.

questions.q: In the reaction of water attacking a carbocation, water acts as a
questions.explanation: The oxygen of water has lone pairs of electrons that it donates to the electron-deficient carbocation, so water behaves as a nucleophile (and a Lewis base) in this step.
questions.trick: Lone pair attacking electron-deficient carbon = water acting as nucleophile.

questions.q: A compound containing only C, H and O gave, on combustion of 0.30 g, 0.44 g of CO$_2$ and 0.18 g of H$_2$O. The percentage of oxygen in the compound is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explanation: %C $= \dfrac{0.44\times12}{44\times0.30}\times100 = 40\%$; %H $= \dfrac{0.18\times2}{18\times0.30}\times100 \approx 6.7\%$. Since only C, H, O are present, %O $= 100-40-6.7 = 53.3\%$.
questions.trick: Find %C and %H from CO$_2$/H$_2$O, then %O = 100 − %C − %H.

questions.q: Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism about a C=C double bond requires that
options: the two doubly bonded carbons must bear identical groups
there must be free rotation about the double bond
each doubly bonded carbon must bear two different groups/atoms
questions.explanation: Restricted rotation about C=C fixes substituent positions; geometrical isomerism arises only when each sp$^2$ carbon of the double bond carries two different groups, as in but-2-ene, but not in propene where one carbon bears two identical H atoms.
questions.trick: cis-trans needs each double-bond carbon to carry two DIFFERENT groups.
